Big Tech Engagement Action Plan
Background: Russian civil society and independent media face significant challenges in
overcoming government censorship and reaching their target audiences inside Russia. This has
been exacerbated by the decisions of private sector tech companies to either stop operating
inside Russia or deny service to Russian passport holders in order to comply with sanctions and
not be seen to promote the war. In some cases, existing and well-meaning policies have similar
effects. While the intent of these policies is sound, denial-of-service policies do not generally
impact supporters of Putin's regime whose enablers can leverage dual citizenship and contacts
abroad to accomplish their goals, but significantly handicap those who oppose the war. This has
required anti-war and democratic actors to spend significant time and resources overcoming
the policies of U.S. tech companies in addition toinstead of countering Kremlin disinformation.
The result is that USAID's partners and others speaking out against the war face effective
censorship from two sides, and are unable to reach audiences that are eager for their
content. They claim that regular channels to contact tech companies about these issues have
not proven fruitful.
The State Department has also heard similar concerns from its partners in this area, and they
have undertaken scattered working-level outreach with tech companies to address some of
them with uncertain success. Due to the number of offices involved, they do not have a
complete accounting of that outreach or how it might conflict with anything proposed in this
action plan.
Current USAID actions:
Interagency Discussion: USAID has discussed this plan with the State Department due to their
own ongoing engagements with tech companies on similar issues relating to their own
partners. They ask that USAID engagement be prefaced by an interagency discussion through
the NSC to decide on a more unified policy for approaching companies; this can be
accomplished through existing sub-IPC processes. USAID should maintain a policy to support
our partners by approaching tech companies when they ask us to do so.
The primary recommendation in this plan to create an inclusion list of trusted actors has been
discussed internally at State and opposed because of concerns about representing specific
actions or actors to receive special treatment as the U.S. government, raising freedom of

expression issues. What we propose here is not a list that would be curated by any U.S.
department or agency, but rather to connect tech companies with actors that we trust who
would be willing to curate an inclusion list on behalf of any companies that are willing to follow
one. We recognize that it is up to the companies to determine for themselves whether and how
to implement any policies with regard to an inclusion list curated by a third party.
Key Recommendation 1: Tech companies implement an inclusion list for verified actors. These
lists should be private and managed in a decentralized manner through trusted third-party
implementers, which are already interlocutors with the tech companies on similar issues in
other countries. ASK companies how to create an inclusion list using 3rd party curators/verifiers
that results in maximum response and requires minimal level of effort from tech companies.
Key Recommendation 2: Companies should avoid opening offices ('landing') inside Russia as it
increases the Russian government's ability to coerce companies to comply with censorship
measures.
Key Recommendation 3: Tech companies should consider working collectively to fight
authoritarian cyber-censorship and propaganda as outlined in a proposal by Nobel prize
winner Dmitry Muratov and other journalists to create a community of "Engineers Against
Dictatorship."
Prioritized Company Recommendations:
1. Alphabet
a. YouTube:
Issue: YouTube has deactivated monetization for anyone located in Russia and
for any views that occur in Russia.
Recommendation: Online publishers should allow organizations on the inclusion
list to monetize their content inside Russia.
Issue: CSOs and independent media can't target or advertise content to
audiences inside Russia.
Recommendation: Allow organizations on the inclusion list to buy and publish
ads in Russia and target content to users in Russia.
b. Google:

Issue: Websites blocked in Russia are being downgraded in search results. Search
algorithms register user behavior such as whether a user who clicked on a search
result returns to the results page (i.e. they didn't find what they were looking
for). If so, the page is considered a low quality result. If a website is blocked, then
many users return to the search results. This sends a false signal to the search
engine and search algorithms become amplifiers of censorship.
Recommendation: Search engines should not downgrade pages belonging to
entities on the inclusion list for reasons related to blocking. Search engines
should also warn users that websites belonging to entities on the inclusion list
may be blocked and offer recommendations for VPNs or other circumvention
technology to bypass the blocking.
Issue: Google's recommendation algorithms (Google Discover in particular -
detail here) promote those articles that have the most likes. This gives advantage
to the official media. The same algorithms demote independent media with an
anti-war agenda.
Recommendation 1: review recommendation algorithms to ensure they do not
promote pro-war or government controlled content (could be identified with the
use of natural language models with high precision as prototyped by ENP 2.0
partners). Review algorithms to ensure that entities on the inclusion list are not
demoted for spurious reasons.
Recommendation 2: Analyze the effect of bot-attacks and bot-manipulations on
recommendation algorithms. Activists and experts suspect that the domination
of recommendation algorithms by propaganda may be connected to big tech's
inability to defend itself from bot manipulations (e.g. thousands of bots like
state-sponsored propaganda pieces thus bringing it up to the top-10 of
recommended content). It is believed that big tech could do better when it
comes to combating automatic inauthentic behavior (bots).
Issue: Google receives content take-down requests from the Russian authorities
on a regular basis. Since March 2022, these requests have usually not been
approved.
Recommendation: Google should continue to deny these requests. Google
could also publish take-down requests or provide them to the academic
community to support anti-censorship and anti-authoritarian research. This data,

now accumulated by the large companies, could be used to promote knowledge
on authoritarian practices.
c. Google Play
Issue: Apps published by exiled media are attacked by bots on a regular basis
leading to poor ratings.
Recommendation:
2. Meta (Facebook and Instagram):
Issue: CSOs and media can't target or advertise content to audiences in Russia.
Recommendation: Allow organizations on the inclusion list to buy and publish ads in
Russia and target content to users in Russia. Because the use of VPNs obscures user

Issue: Recommendation algorithms demote organically created anti-war related content

Recommendation: Review recommendation algorithms and minimize the possibility of

CENTER FOR
INNOVATION
AND IMPACT
©USAID | Global Health
Leveraging the Private Sector for the COVID-19 Response Concept Note
Vaccine Information & Community Engagement through Facebook and
WhatsApp
Summary
Leverage the network, reach, and influence of Facebook and its associated 1:1 communication channels
like WhatsApp to improve the distribution of accurate COVID-19 information, spark demand for the
COVID vaccine, and create positive information campaigns to reduce vaccine hesitancy.
Problem Statement
Many countries are facing a high level of COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy, rampant mis or disinformation
about COVID in general, and related to its vaccines, cures, treatments, or the origins of the virus, and
mistrust in public health agencies or governments. In many places, these issues are resulting in
insufficient demand for the COVID vaccine, improper use of masks, limited social distancing, and low
levels of testing, reporting, or quarantining. Combined, these challenges can significantly impede a
sub-national, national, and global response to COVID.
Proposal
Use Facebook's COVID Vaccine Information Center, ad campaigns, Data for Good program, and
WhatsApp chatbots to disseminate accurate and timely information regarding COVID at the sub-national
level, promote positive ad and media public health campaigns, and conduct robust M&E on the success
of these efforts. These tools can help Ministries of Health and other government departments leverage
the power of Facebook's multiple platforms and wide audience to enhance community engagement,
generate demand for the COVID vaccine, and distribute information that can lead to appropriate action.
Main offerings
Facebook has engaged in many activities to combat COVID-19 and further the spread of accurate and
timely information about the disease. One initiative included making the WHO website accessible to
users in low-and-middle-income countries (LMICs) without incurring data charges. Other initiatives that
Facebook offers or can offer LMIC governments include:
• Connecting people to reliable information about COVID-19 vaccines, through:
• Use of the COVID Information Center, which is live in over 200 countries and has been
translated into over 70 languages. This center enables Facebook users to get local
information at scale by showcasing information from local, national, regional and global
health authorities.

• Delivery of ad credits and media space to Ministries of Health or other public health
organizations that are putting out health messaging. So far, Facebook has given more
than $30 million in ad credits to help governments, NGOs, and other organizations reach
people with COVID-19 vaccine information and other important messages. These
information campaigns resulted in an estimated 10 billion ad impressions globally.
• A sample COVID-19 vaccine campaign structure for a country can include several
stages, beginning with awareness:
• Phase 1: Build vaccine confidence amongst the general public by
distributing the national vaccine rollout plan, facts about vaccine safety,
ingredients, and population prioritization
• Phase 2: Alert high-risk group 60+ in four regions by sending information
about vaccine availability, registration sites, and vaccination locations
• Phase 3: Register priority group for vaccinations by driving registrations
on MoH or other website
• Phase 4: Remind and reinforce behavior by sending reminders about
registrations, vaccination dates, and locations
Facebook can work with a country to tailor messages for the citizens of that country,
such as encouraging vaccine registrations, social distancing, wearing masks, etc. This
approach is similar to what Facebook has done in the past for certain countries by
reminding individuals in a country to vote around the time of elections.
• Conducting M&E to help drive decision-making and policy-making in LMICs:
• Facebook can support ad evaluations to help decision-makers see how effective their
advertisement campaigns and messages are at encouraging individuals to display
health-seeking behavior such as mask-wearing or vaccine registrations.
Facebook'sData for Good program has been implementing a COVID survey for over a
year now with over 200 countries, collecting incredibly valuable information around the
key drivers of vaccine hesitancy, mask usage, and uptake of behaviors. See visualizations
nere.
• Leveraging WhatsApp for push messaging:
• Given the ubiquity of WhatsApp in LMICs, Facebook has worked with the WHO and
governments to access their API, working with developer partners to create chatbots for
governments to promote health-related content.
• For example, Facebook worked with the Ministry of Health in Buenos Aires,
Argentina to create a chatbot around COVID testing availability and COVID
vaccines, so users receive a notification that gives them a phone number to get
MoH information on WhatsApp and a number to text to receive information.
This approach enables user-initiated messaging and empowers citizens to take
control over their own health in a secured and end-to-end encrypted platform.

Since the start of the pandemic, WhatsApp has partnered with more than 150 national,
state, and local governments, and with organizations like WHO and UNICEF, on COVID-19
helplines to connect over 2 billion users to accurate information and resources. Over 3
billion messages have been sent across these global helplines in the past year.
As the pandemic enters a new phase in many countries, governments are using these
helplines to connect citizens privately to accurate vaccine information and registration,
in countries such as Indonesia, South Africa, Argentina, Brazil, and India. In Indonesia,
500,000 medical workers registered for their vaccine appointments on this service in its
first 5 days.
WhatsApp wants to help governments and international organizations connect as many

Introduction
Even though social media plays a critical role in facilitating access to information while empowering ordinary citizens
to produce contents that matter to them, it is also used to fuel hate, conflict, polarization and disinformation [8].
Identifying these digital threats and protecting users from online abuse have drawn the attention of researchers,
advocates, policymakers, and social media companies. However, the response by social media companies whose very
platforms are used to spread such content has been complicated by the lack of accord on the boundaries of acceptable
online conduct [9].
Reliably mapping digital threats on social media platforms, hence, requires a distinct strategy in the monitoring and
documentation of harmful online content. As most of GIF's partners [10] are human rights defenders, civil society
actors and journalists from close to 50 countries who advocate for an inclusive, safe, and open Internet, this
methodology is framed to accommodate the respective needs and end-goals of this diverse partnership.
While this methodology document seeks to provide partners with the tools to identify, document and report harmful
speech, it is expected to eventually lead to a large entry of important datasets that could potentially indicate the most
suitable line of action to counter online harmful speech. Additionally, the interrelationships between these harmful
sentiments and their corresponding offline harms can be accurately analyzed, then used by partners to promote
effective local and transnational solutions.
In developing this methodology document, GIF analyzed relevant studies that have been conducted on the topic and
found that there is generally one main approach for monitoring and documenting harmful content online. The
approach entails identifying and cataloguing keywords andthe user accounts of bad actors onto a versatile template,
while providing historical, linguistic as well as other relevant context about each item of relevant content. This
approach can be adjusted to meet the specific needs of the researcher, depending on the prevalence of the online
harm and its offline manifestation.
Scope
This document presents a digital threat tracking and mapping methodology that aims to enable external partners to
aptly identify, track and report harmful social media contents. However, understanding the definitions of the terms
and expressions pertinent to digital threats and building a rich context thereof should precede tracking and mapping
activities.
The key justification for studying these definitions is that understanding the cultural and linguistic nuances of these
terms and expressions within the online space in question plays an exclusive role in reliably mapping the social media
landscape where groups and communities are being targeted
Cognizant of its expansive domain, therefore, a decision was made to develop this methodology based on the two
most important topics of online harmful practices - hate speech and online violence. Because limiting the purview of
this document would enhance its potency, it focuses on the three social media platforms that a majority of online
users choose to access digital news contents from - Facebook, Twitter and YouTube [29].
Accordingly, from the many forms of digital threats, this methodology focuses on how partners can build a
comprehensive knowledge, understanding and analysis of the impact of hate speech and online violence within their
respective regions so that an effective data-driven advocacy can be crafted. However, depending on specific needs,
this methodology can also be adapted to address other forms of harmful practices.
Challenges in Defining Hate Speech
To understand how experts characterize hate speech and to acquire cumulative interpretations of hate speech and
its impacts, it is important to look at the most notable terminologies and how they are defined in academic, legal and
policy literature. Ideally, having an unequivocal definition of hate speech would allow for a coherent way of dealing
2

with its online and offline manifestations, which can also be used to address specific problems with the right
contextual awareness.
Seeking to produce a
"legal literature" that aimed to define hate speech and hate crime, a group of researchers
conducted a systematic review on the evolution and status of hate speech [27]. The group reviewed research papers
that were written in English and Spanish, which studied hate speech from legal and communication standpoints.
According to the review, academic interest in hate speech grew from 42 to 162 in five years (2013 - 2018), measured
by the volume of indexed papers produced on the Web of Science, the world's first citation index. Unfortunately, hate
speech remains one of the most important topics that lacks uniform legal definition across countries and institutions.
According to the United Nations, for example, there is no universal definition [24] of hate speech under the
International Human Rights Law because the concept is still disputed based on freedom of opinion and expression.
Nevertheless, the UN provides a definition under a framework known as United Nations Strategy and Plan of Action,
which defines hate speech as:
"Any kind of communication in speech, writing or behaviour, thatattacks or uses pejorative or
discriminatory language with reference to a person or a group on the basis of who they are, in other words,
based on their religion, ethnicity, nationality, race, colour, descent, gender or other identity factor."
The UN elaborates that hate speech can be expressed through images, cartoons, memes, objects, gestures and
symbols, which often generate intolerance, hatred and, in certain contexts, can be demeaning and divisive. It notes
that these expressions are not considered hate speech if they are directed against States and their offices or symbols,
public officials, or religious leaders or tenets of faith.
On the other hand, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) [34] defines hate
speech even more cautiously. In a study it developed in cooperation with the Programme in Comparative Media Law
and Policy (PCMLP) at the University of Oxford, UNESCO insists that any collateral restriction of legitimate expression
in response to and while identifying and limiting hate speech would not be justifiable. Nevertheless, this study states
that speech can be identified as hate speech (whether it is expressed through text, image, or sound) by its degrading
and dehumanizing purpose against members assigned to a targeted group.
Similarly, the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) [25] held a series of expert seminars
between 2008 and 2012 to deliberate on the prohibition of incitement to national, racial or religious hatred, in which
it adopted the Rabat Plan of Action, a document it called a "practical and useful tool" in the fight against incitement
to hatred and violence. The Rabat Plan of Action, which has since been translated in 32 languages, outlines a six-part
threshold test to identify hate speech, namely:
1. Context: The social and political context of the speech,
2. Speaker: Status of the speaker,
Intent: the intent to incite the audience against a target group,
4.
Content and form: the content and form of the speech,
5. Extent: Extent of the speech's dissemination, reach and magnitude,
6. Likelihood and imminence: the likelihood of harm, including imminence.
The action plan suggests that all of six parts of the threshold test need to be fulfilled for a statement to be considered
as an offence so that the limitations to freedom of expression remain an exception.
In line with the UN and its specialized agencies, scholarly journals and researchers also exhibit identical caution when
it comes to defining hate speech. In its mapping review of approaches to defining and measuring hate speech, a
journal by Campbell Systematic Reviews [35] found that there is a rapid increase of vocabulary used to refer to similar
harmful online behaviours, which, together with the lack of clarity in relevant definitions, pose real challenges to
policy, practice and research.
3

Who is the Authority on Hate Speech then?
Amid the challenges caused by nuanced and pronounced definition differences, the question remains, who is the
arbiter for determining hate speech? While one of the main reasons all the institutions defining hate speech found
the task to be complex is its delicateintersection with freedom of expression, another practical issue is the lack of
jurisdictional control over online content. The increasing speed with which content spreads on the Internet makes it
challenging for state actors to execute national laws on online platforms. In some instances, governments have taken
regulatory measures [15] that pressed tech companies to take more responsibility in enforcing relevant laws.
However, such measures are limited in their applicability, which has so far allowed social media platforms' community
standards to largely remain the governing principles regarding user practices. Ironically, because social media
companies continue to rely on users to flag problematic content such as hate speech, users have essentially become
the authority who have the last word. Hence, the role of the media, human rights advocates and local institutions
becomes irreplaceable in raising public awareness about the roles and responsibilities they hold in making the virtual
world free and safe. Therefore, it is essential to outline the community standards provided by some of the popular
social media platforms.
META
Instagram's community guidelines states that "it is never OK to encourage violence or attack anyone based on their
race, ethnicity, national origin, sex, gender, gender identity, sexual orientation, religious affiliation, disabilities or
diseases." On the other hand, Facebook's community standards [13] state that people will freely connect if they do
not feel attacked based on who they are. And to that effect, it defines hate speech as a direct attack against people
based on what it calls protected characteristics: race, ethnicity, national origin, disability, religious affiliation, caste,
sexual orientation, sex, gender identity and serious disease. By 'attack' it is referring to violent or dehumanizing
speech, harmful stereotypes, statements of inferiority, expressions of contempt, disgust or dismissal, cursing and
calls for exclusion or segregation. It also prohibits harmful stereotypes, which it describes as dehumanizing
comparisons that have historically been used to attack, intimidate, or exclude specific groups, and that are often
linked with offline violence.
TWITTER
Twitter's [31] policy on hateful content, similarly, prohibits the promotion of violence against or direct attacks on or
threats to other people based on race, ethnicity, national origin, caste, sexual orientation, gender, gender identity,
religious affiliation, age, disability, or serious disease. Its policy indicates that women, people of color, lesbian, gay,
bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual individuals, marginalized and historically underrepresented
communities are disproportionately targeted with abuse online. The policy expresses its dedication to fighting abuse
that is inspired by hatred, prejudice or intolerance, especially abuse that aims to stifle the voices of those who have
historically been marginalized.
YOUTUBE
The hate speech Community Guidelines by YouTube [14] prohibit content that promotes violence or hatred against
individuals or groups based on their age, caste, disability, ethnicity, gender identity and expression, nationality, race,
immigration status, religion, sex/gender, sexual orientation, victims of a major violent event and their kin and veteran
status. It also does not allow content that encourages violence against individuals or groups based on any of the listed
attributes. Additionally, its guidelines state that threats and implied calls for violence are forbidden.
Defining Online Violence
The United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) [1] uses the term digital violence to describe a similar abuse, though it
admits there are many other expressions for it. According to a study it attributed to the Economist Intelligence Unit,
85% of women globally have been exposed to or experienced some form of online violence, and nearly 40% have
experienced it personally. The UN agency defines online violence as "an act of violence perpetrated by one or more
individuals that is rooted in gender inequality and gendered norms and that is committed, assisted, aggravated and
amplified in part or fully by the use of information and communication technologies or digital media, against a person
on the basis of their gender."
4

An online community hub, Tech Without Violence [5], used a different terminology for a similar concept -
cyberviolence. It defines cyberviolence as "online behaviours that criminally or non-criminally assault, or can lead to
assault, of a person's physical, psychological or emotional well-being."
The European Council [4], on the other hand, used cyberviolence in slightly broader context. The council defines it as
"the use of computer systems to cause, facilitate, or threaten violence against individuals, that results in (or is likely
to result in) physical, sexual, psychological or economic harm or suffering and may include the exploitation of the
individual's circumstance, characteristics or vulnerabilities."
As indicated above, the user policies of respective social media platforms are by far the main governing principles
regarding user practices. While it is important to study the different measurements that institutions use to define
hate speech, ultimately the presiding standard is that of the platforms.
META
Meta's policy [36] puts incitement and violence into one category and defines it as an abuse that has a potential offline
harm. These abuses arethreats that could lead to death (and other forms of high-severity violence) and admission of
past violence targeting people or places. The community standard further goes to define 'threat' as follows:
•
Statements of intent to commit high-severity violence,
• Calls for high-severity violence,
• Statements advocating for high-severity violence,
• Aspirational or conditional statements to commit high-severity violence,
• Statements admitting to committing high-severity violence.
TWITTER
Twitter categorises violence into two: Violent Threats [32] and Glorification of Violence [26] acts. It defines violent
threats as "statements of an intent to kill or inflict serious physical harm on a specific person or group of people.
Threatening an individual or a group of people with violence as well as the glorification of violence is prohibited on
the platform. Others in this policy include, but are not limited to:
• Threatening to kill someone,
o Threatening to sexually assault someone,
• Threatening to seriously hurt or lead to someone's death or serious physical injury,
• Asking for or offering a financial reward in exchange for inflicting violence on a specific person or group of people,
o Glorifying, celebrating, praising or condoning violent crimes, violent events where people were targeted because
of their membership in a protected group, or the perpetrators of such acts.
The second category - glorifying violent acts - is contents that "glorify acts of violence in a way that may inspire others
to replicate those violent acts and cause real offline harm, or events where members of a protected group were the
primary targets or victims." According to the platform, glorification is praising, celebrating, or condoning statements
towards:
1. Violent acts committed by civilians that resulted in death or serious physical injury,
2. Attacks carried out by terrorist organizations or violent extremist groups, and
3. Violent events that targeted protected groups
YOUTUBE
Content that seeks to "shock or disgust viewers, or content that encourages others to commit violent acts, are not
allowed on YouTube" [37]. Below are some of types of content that can be categorized as violent behaviour:
• Inciting others to commit violent acts against individuals or a defined group of people.
• Footage, audio, or imagery involving road accidents, natural disasters, war aftermath, terrorist attack aftermath,
street fights, physical attacks, immolation, torture, corpses, protests or riots, robberies, medical procedures, or
other such scenarios with the intent to shock or disgust viewers.
5

o Footage or imagery showing bodily fluids, such as blood or vomit, with the intent to shock or disgust viewers.
• Footage of corpses with massive injuries, such as severed limbs.
Additionally, YouTube does not allow violent or criminal organizations to use the platform "for any purpose, including
recruitment." Users cannot use its platform to praise, promote, or aid these organizations.
Troll Farms and Inauthentic Behaviours
With the advancement of artificial intelligence, social media is no longer reserved for only human users. Studies
suggest that bots and automated accounts are increasingly being used to shape public opinion. [21]
UNDP published a research paper comparing organizations based in 28 countries, in which it found that these
organizations had deployed cyber troops to operate fake accounts that flooded online platforms with spam and fake
content. [21
"Many different countries employ significant numbers of people and resources to manage and manipulate public
opinion online, sometimes targeting domestic audiences and sometimes targeting foreign publics," the paper adds,
while explaining the omnipresent nature of cyber troops. These troops, backed by trolls and bots, produce content
on fake social media accounts to artificially amplify the reach and influence of content that is mostly harmful.
Similarly, according to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), these entities, called troll factories, often
conceal their identity to "achieve their goals using, among other things, fake news and hate speech." [23] The term
'troll factory' began to gain traction in 2015, NATO's modest brochure affirms.
"Since the troll factory employs hundreds of people and each employee has several accounts, it is easy to create a
social network linking fake profiles and the impression of a real one. The longer the given accounts are maintained,
the easier it is to create the illusion of reality," it adds.
Another term that Meta created to describe inauthenticity is CIB, short for Coordinated Inauthentic Behaviour. Meta
defines such accounts as "groups of pages or people to mislead others about who they are or what they're doing."
[16] According to the platform, these behaviours rely on fake accounts and other inauthentic tactics to drive traffic
and mislead people while most of the content promotes dangerous, harmful, or hateful content.
The problem, Meta adds, "is that the actors behind these campaigns are using deceptive behaviours to conceal the
identity of the organization behind a campaign, making the organization or itsactivity appear more popular or
trustworthy than it is, or evade our enforcement efforts."
Monitoring Online Content
Analysing raw data is only as good as the data itself. Patchy, imprecise, or inconsistent data could lead to an analysis
that is incomplete, or worse, misleading. Below is a list of tips that would serve as an initial starting point to
systematically approach the tracking and documentation of online content. It will help practitioners to develop
datasets and benchmarks to analyze and contextualize online harms as well as to indicate ways that prevent offline
harms caused by online content.
To that end, this methodology studied a few initiatives that had impactful monitoring and documentation works across
the world. In India, Equality Labs [28] published a report that discusses the threats against Indian minorities in India
and abroad. The report provided essential data, analysis and recommendations following a six-month research project
that monitored the prevalence of hate speech against minorities based on caste, religion, and gender on Facebook.
In Kenya, the Umati [33] project set out to monitor online content and record incidents of hate and dangerous speech
after it found out there is a need to define, identify and deal with dangerous speech during the 2013 elections.
According to the report it published immediately after the elections, the project sought to identify and understand
the use of dangerous speech online, which recommended non-government solutions to the offline harms it created.
6

This methodology aims to expand on these extensive and focused research projects so that a comprehensive
monitoring, identification and reporting tool is available to support future researches.
Digital threat identifier
Monitoring and identifying digital threats require a sustained effort so that accurate and reliable datasets are built.
Furthermore, investigating these threats should be done in a way that ensures accurate results within an environment
that is both safe and comfortable for the researcher. Having a dedicated social media account for such tasks is,
therefore, advisable so that partners can stay away from unwarranted exposures and incidents.
The other reason to having a separate account is that of the personalized algorithms that social media platforms
implement on news feeds to improve their user experience, whose parameters are, by and large, criticized for their
biases. A case study [11] done in 2018 on the Italian elections found that Facebook's News Feed algorithms tend to
reinforce "likes" by filtering and favouring those posts among the available contents. The study concluded that this
bias is 'non-negligible' even for users who have a 'neutral" political view. And to avoid the limitation caused by such
types of platform-imposed biases, insulating accounts pertinent to this task is advantageous.
According to a cross-national perspective provided in the book, Online Hate and Harmful Content, hate, motivated by
prejudice, can be expressed in speech and in action with which an individual or a group is targeted. "Extreme acts
such as mass murders or terrorist attacks are manifestations of hate," it adds (18].
When it comes to identifiers, most digital threats relevant to hate speech and online violence share common
characteristics when they manifest online. These are some of the notable identifiers of hate speech:
1. The content targets a group, or an individual as a member of a group,
2. There is a dehumanizing sentiment within the content,
3. The content encourages and justifies a collective self-defence, which is also known as 'accusation in mirror'
4. There is a call to action in the content - murder, violence, segregation, discrimination, xenophobia and others.

Circumventing content moderation
Today, it is estimated that there are about 4.76 billion active social media users in the world - almost 60% of the total
global population - exchanging billions on contents daily.
And growing number of social media users are now utilizing nefarious tactics to circumvent automated content
moderation so that their content can remain online even if it is in violation of the platform's user policies. And while
platforms' response to ensure compliance with their policies and community standards has arguably been reactive,
the use of Artificial Intelligence against problematic contents is gaining momentum in influencing decision-making
process of content moderations.
And learning the tactics and strategies that such social media users employ to evade moderation algorithms would
help us identify the pitfalls that make identifying harmful contents more challenging. Some of these tactics and
strategies include:
• Using ciphered language,
• Using keywords with lexical variations,
• Visual blocking of keywords in images (superimposing texts over images),
• The use of alphanumeric characters,
• Using screenshots instead of textual content or links,
• Putting additional information in comment section,
• Using the likeness of prominent personality and institution to spread harmful content,
• Camouflage malicious content within harmless looking links/ads (also known as "cloaking"),
• Using neutral or semi-neutral hashtags with borderline provocative tone,
• Switching totemporary or short contents such as Facebook/Instagram Story andunrecorded Twitter Space,
• Redirecting users using third party features such as Linktree and Bio,
Briefly flashing harmful imagery within a longer video,
• Streaming harmful contents live,
It is worth noting that researchers engaged in monitoring and tracking harmful content can progressively learn to
better identify such behaviours by upskilling themselves while using a combination of technical and social research
skills. Additionally, some sophisticated attempts may require researchers to be vigilant and maintain high-level
awareness about local and international affairs so that they can consistently and reliably identify trends that could
trigger harmful content to come into being.
It is important to work collaboratively with partners, stakeholders and other researchers to develop effective
strategies for monitoring and tracking harmful content. Below is a list of non-exhaustive points that researchers may
consider as part of an effective monitoring and tracking strategy:
1. Having a comprehensive knowledge of user policies and community guidelines will help researchers identify
behaviours that are prohibited and provide a framework for assessing content on respective platforms.
9

2. When possible, use third-party tools and technologies that can help identify patterns of behaviour that are
suspicious or anomalous. For example, there are inexpensive monitoring tools that use effective machine
learning algorithms to identify language patterns that may indicate a user is attempting to circumvent Al
moderations.
3. While using automated third-party monitoring tools, researchers can put in place filters (also known as rules)
that are programmed to send instant notifications when selected keywords appear on the platforms being
monitored.
4. Monitor social media platforms for changes in behaviour, especially when during changes and high-profile
events. For example, during an election cycle or a period of civil unrest, you may see an increase in users
attempting to utilize tactics to circumvent content moderation.
5. Look for inconsistencies in content, such as sudden spikes in activity or unusual patterns of behaviour that
may indicate coordinated or malicious activity.
6. Engage with the social media community to gather insights into how users may be attempting to circumvent
content moderation. Interactions such as comments, shares and retweets could provide valuable insights
into the strategies bad actors are employing.
7. Look for specific attributes of the content, which could be regarded as typical evasive behaviours :
• Language: patterns of coded language or ambiguous references may be used to evade detection by
algorithms or human moderators.
• Context: examine the context in which content is posted, such as the time, location, or user
demographics, to identify patterns that may indicate coordinated or malicious activity.
• Amplification: a content could be amplified through fake accounts or third-party services to evade
detection.
• Image or video manipulation: Look for alterations or manipulations of images or videos that may be used
to evade detection by algorithms that recognize explicit or hate speech content.
• Evasive tactics: a content could use tactics like conceal offensive content in seemingly innocent posts or
comments.
• User behaviour: Monitor the behaviour of individual users to identify patterns such as cross-posting
multiple contents rapidly, using multiple accounts, Keyword Stuffing (artificially boost the relevance of
a piece of content for a particular keyword or phrase).
In summary, it is important to approach this task with a critical eye and remain objective throughout the process. It is
also essential to prioritize user privacy and not engage in activities that may violate user rights or lead to unethical
research practices. Ultimately, the goal of monitoring online content is to identify, track and document problematic
content, while promoting a safe and positive online environment for all users.

Protecting the privacy and identity of individuals who monitor and track online contents is crucial to ensure their

4. Use secure communication channels: everyone involved should use secure communication channels to
communicate with each other as well as stakeholders, such as end-to-end encrypted messaging apps.

can take a toll on their mental health. Mental health support should be available to help them cope with
potential consequence of emotional and psychological distress.
6.
Regularly update privacy policies: the privacy and safety policies should regularly be reviewed and updated
to ensure that they remain effective in protecting the privacy and identity.

set dashboards - like Talkwalker IQ Apps - and customizable dashboards help you to see all the metrics and
analytics you need in one place.
• Virality Maps: These maps show where and when messages spread and which sources were most important in
helpingthem spread. They help you understand why and how a particular post, tweet or article spread across
social media and online.
• Spike Analysis: It involves focusing on particular spikes in mentions and then drilling down into the data to
understand why such an event occurred. This type of analysis is particularly useful to understand the causes of
a crisis, why certain campaigns were successful and to better understand the types of posts, stories and
campaigns that capture the social public's attention.
Step 5: Report
Once insights have been uncovered, the final step is reporting. Having good reporting functions is critical as they not
only allow you to distribute insights to all relevant stakeholders, but being able to create reports quickly also helps to
save the time needed for analysis and reporting, according to Talkwalker's client tests.
All relevant charts/graphs can be selected for inclusion in a report and then scheduled on a daily, weekly or monthly
basis. Creating alerts based on irregular activity also helps to warn you of an impending crisis or an unexpected positive
event.

NewsWhip is a real-time media monitoring platform, which combines real-time feeds of web and social content with
public engagement data to identify and predict the content that matters. The platform uses advanced algorithms and
data analytics techniques to track the performance of online content across a variety of outlets, including social media,
websites and blogs.

It can be used for media monitoring, crisis management, as well as research and strategy. According to the platform,
its users range from journalists, content strategists, marketing executives, social media managers, and so on, across
various industries. In general, to start using the NewsWhip platform,you are required to purchase membership to
create an account and connect your social media accounts or other sources of media content. Once you have done
that, you can access the tool's features and metrics to track and analyze the performance of your content. This may
involve using the tool's dashboard, setting up alerts and notifications, or creating custom reports and visualizations.
Pricing: There is very little information about the pricing plan and model that is offered by NewsWhip, and it

The following beginners' guide can be used as a starting point:
1. Subscribe and log in to NewsWhip website,
2. Create dashboards that will enable you to view multiple widgets for one or more searches simultaneously
Widgets are the constitutional parts of a dashboard that let you choose how to view and display the results
of your searches. Widgets can be mixed and matched across searches and dashboards to suit your needs.
There are three main types of widgets that this platform employs:
Feeds widgets: They present a feed of posts from the different platforms we track. This includes all web
articles and social media, including Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, Reddit, and YouTube.
Leaderboard widgets: These widgets gather data from across many posts and present that on an aggregate

Timeline widget: This widget shows how the media and public have engaged with a given topic over a

is developing and evolving over time.
3. The easiest way to get started is to use a preconfigured template with one of its three curated searches. The
platform offers three separate templates that can also be selected for a custom search or with one of the
platform's curated searches, which can give you access to a library of pre-built searches, ranging from key
events, to topics, to trends that may be of interest to you. The three templates that can be optimized for
their respective use case are:
Monitoring Template: This template is ideal for monitoring a topic across the web and all major social
networks.
Crisis Template: This can be used to track how media and public interest in a crisis is evolving.
Research Template: This is best used to understand how interest in an event or topic is changing over time.

options, among which is sorting by a time range where it can be configured by custom date range.
5. After refining the topics to search, begin working on the filters, including sources of information, language,
locations and more.
6. After adding your search and refining it further to meet your needs, follow the basic rules of building a search
to get the most accurate data as quickly as possible. This involves creating targeted search queries that can
be done in one of the three ways: by keywords, by sources or by using URL links. It is important to understand
the power of using the Boolean Search technique, which connects individual keywords or phrases within a
single query in a number of ways.

Tableau
Monitoring harmful contents posted on social media can be done with Tableau, an intelligence and data visualization
application. Utilizing its data analytics and visualization tools, it is possible to examine social media data and spot
potentially dangerous information. The text of messages can be examined using its text analysis and sentiment
analysis functions; for instance, to find posts with potentially objectionable or dangerous content. With the help of
Tableau, you can make a range of dynamic and aesthetically pleasing data graphs and dashboards.
Additionally, Tableau's geospatial analysis tools can be used to spot regional patterns and trends in social media data,
which can be utilized to pinpoint regions with a higher concentration of dangerous content. Tableau's dashboarding
and reporting features can be used to build interactive visualizations and reports that assist in monitoring and tracking
the spread of potentially hazardous content on social media once the possible harmful content has been recognized
Pricing: Tableau's subscription plans are divided into three categories: Tableau Creator (USD70/mo.), Tableau Explorer
(USD42/mo.), and Tableau Viewer (USD15/mo.).
Here is a step-by-step guide on how Tableau can be used to monitor harmful content on social media:
1.
On Tableau's website, subscribe and create an account,
2. Once logged in, go to the "Connect" tab and select the data source that you want to track. There are two
ways to do this: use the built-in connectors for popular social media platforms such as Twitter and Facebook,
or import data from a CSV or similar data file.
3. Go to the "Data" tab and drag and drop the relevant columns into the workspace, which creates a visual
representation of the connected data, such as a bar chart or scatter plot.

• Removing data that are irrelevant and unnecessary,
• Merging data that came from various sources, and
• Creating new parameters and measurements.
5. By selecting the "Filters" tab, refine the data by selecting the relevant criteria that would potentially return
the specified contents, actors, keywords, phrases, social media platforms, languages, or locations.
6. In the "Analytics" section, go to the "Create Calculated Field", which enables you to track the performance
of the selected filters, such as the number of likes, comments or shares.
7. The dashboard, while using it to monitor the contents and actors, can be configured to send notifications
when certain conditions are met to your preferred address. These configurations can be set in a way that
alerts are sent to you when, for example, a specified number of harmful posts are identified in a specific
geographic area. This ideal feature helps in the automation of tracking accounts and users even outside of
your normal working hours, which can help you to respond quickly to potential crisis situations.

collected data. This is a built-in feature that uses word clouds and key phrase extraction techniques to identify
common terms and phrases that may hold negative or offensive sentiment.
9. By using its geospatial analytics feature, you can identify the geographical patterns and trends found within
the collected data. This feature can also create maps and other visualization means that show the geographic
distribution of your data, as well as any other patterns that may be relevant to your analysis.

11. Tableau also has collaboration features where you can share data about your findings with others - team

Brandwatch
Brandwatch is a social media monitoring and analytics platform that can help researchers to monitor, track and
analyse social media content. The platform uses algorithms and natural language processing (NLP) to collect data from
various online sources. This data is then organized and analyzed to produce analysis and insights.
One of the key benefits of using Brandwatch is that it allows its users to track and analyze large volumes of data in
real-time. This is very helpful as it enables them to understand the depth and spread of sentiments behind a harmful
content, which in turn allows for quick response time. Additionally, Brandwatch provides visualization tools, including
customizable dashboards, sentiment analysis, and real-time alerts:
1. Customizable dashboards: You can create personalized dashboards that display the most relevant data and
metrics, which makes it easy to monitor and track contents using distinct indicators and their changes in
time.
2.
Sentiment analysis: The platform uses algorithms and NLP to analyse sentiments to categorize them as
positive, negative, or neutral. This allows researchers to quickly identify trends and understand how people
are reacting to the sentiments.
3.
Notifications and Alerts: The platform can be configured to send notifications and alerts when specific
keywords or phrases are mentioned online.

for small businesses. The essentials package, which it recommends is suitable for one to two users, is priced at $108
per month. However, it has not provided pricing information for its other packages that appear to have a quotation-
based pricing model.

the following:
1. Sign up for a Brandwatch account and log in to the platform.
2. Identify the specific type of content you seek tomonitor by specifying it, whether it is hateful content,
cyberbullying, or harassment.
3. Next, define the criteria for your monitoring activity on the dashboard. Use keywords, phrases, actors, or
similar parameters to define and set up the criteria. Try using specific words and their common misspellings
associated with the type of content you seek to monitor, which should also include their sources (such as
social media platforms, websites, blogs...).
4. Use the platform's keyword filters to set up alerts to help you quickly identify and flag any potential harmful
contents.

well as actors that match your monitoring criteria.

Advocacy
Monitoring and tacking of harmful contents or actors cannot be an end by itself. Social media researchers and
advocacy groups, for example, can use the data that these tools generate to create effective community advocacy
campaigns by employing targeted messaging coupled with outreaching efforts in raising awareness about the offline
harm of the online contents.
On the other hand, however, the verifiable datasets and the subsequent contextual analysis present an opportunity
for researchers to advocate for standards and policy changes within the social media platforms. And because the
produced information is expected to be credible that is backed by data, positively engaging with social media
platforms towards better and relevant policies could be possible.
There are several practical measures that advocacy groups can take to launch an effective campaign using the
contextually accurate data analytics produced with the help of these social media monitoring and tracking tools. The
measures, among others, should include:
1. Clearly defining the specific objectives of the campaign,
2. Developing a clear message that addresses the concerns of the victims,
3. Preparing a detailed plan of action on how to use the data analytics to garner social backing for the campaign,
4. Engaging directly with social media platforms by providing evidences of flaws in their policy and practices,
5. Being thoroughly prepared to respond to challenges from various actors, including social media users during the
6. Maintaining a constructive and transparent engagement with social media users, influencers and other
stakeholders about the process that is guiding the campaign efforts,
7. Publishing reports, educational and awareness raising resources based on the initially set goals and objectives,
8. Using the same tools to monitor the effectiveness of the campaign and make necessary strategical adjustments.

Internews
Local voices. Global change.
Media and Human Rights in Southeast Asia
USAID YouTube Collaboration
Background
During their recent meeting, Administrator Power and YouTube CEO Susan Wojcicki discussed
the potential of a formal partnership to support independent journalists through leveraging
YouTube's revenue sharing model and platform. Given the success of independent and
mainstream journalists on YouTube across nearly all geographies, and USAID's support for
civil society and independent media around the world, we are seeking to develop and launch
a formal partnership between our organizations in H2 2022, to advance our shared objectives.
Proposal
Given these shared values and interests, YouTube and USAID are launching an independent
media partnership program to support independent media across the world. This program is
dedicated to spotlighting and growing independent media on our platform, by giving them
access to resources and training to help them thrive on YouTube.
USAID RDMA has already established a project with Internews is Southeast Asia and has asked
Internews to consider how this project can align the USAID/YouTube partnership.
Proposed Internews Scope of Work
Activity 1 - "Pre-bunking" Support to Journalists, Civil Society
Internews will gather journalists, civil society factcheckers and researchers from across SEA
to identify existing cleavages and narratives around which disinformation will likely arise and
which groups are most susceptible to those narratives. Research materials and reporting
guides addressing these identified narratives will be shared through country and regional
level networks to assist media to proactively address concerns or respond quickly and
responsibly as topics are raised in public discourse. There will be two cohorts of 25
participants, 50 in total, with each participant attending a total of four trainings: two in person
and two online trainings. During the first two in person meetings, participants will develop
the SoW for Activity 2 Research and Needs Assessment - Online Video Practice Among SEA
Media and Civil Society. USAID and YouTube will be invited to participate in some of these
sessions.
Outputs: Four regional stakeholder meetings (two in person) with a total of 50 participants
(25 participants per meeting X 2)

Internews
Local voices. Global change.
RDMA Synergy This activity is expanded, the two cohorts were originally planned for just
two online meetings now they will have an in-person meeting to kick off the project and a
follow up online meeting.
Activity 2 - Research and Needs Assessment - Online Video Practice Among SEA Media and
Civil Society
Internews will conduct research with media and civil society partners from across SEA to
understand their use of online video and identify potential needs and opportunities. For
independent newsrooms and civil society organizations engaged in advocacy, video can be an
important channel to engage with audiences and expand reach,impact and potentially
revenue. This research will seek to understand what platforms SEA partners are already using
and document their experiences, including successes and challenges. Topics will range from
audience engagement and monetization to safety and the practicalities of video production.
The report will inform project activities, provide a baseline for evaluation, and shape wider
strategy when it comes to training and investment in video programming in the region.
Outputs: One report outlining current online video practice of SEA Media and Civil Society
partners, which identifies needs and provides strategic recommendations.
Activity 3 - Training of Trainers - Understanding Online Video
This Training of Trainers will provide selected media and civil society participants with an up-
to-date understanding of online video, equipping them to bring skills back to
their
organizations and networks. A key focus of the TOT will be on strategies around online video,
and how to evaluate if these approaches are tailored for individual organizations. The training
will include topics such as audience engagement and monetization. Whilst all video platforms
will be covered, the TOT will be co-facilitated by YouTube who will run a deep-dive session
into the features of their platform. The focus of the TOT will be on the use of online video for
news and advocacy, and the understanding of platform mechanics covered in the training that
will also be relevant to Activity 5 Disinformation Investigations. Finally, it is anticipated there
may be some crossover in the participants. Fellowships will be available for TOT participants
to hone skills developed during the training. Grantees will have the opportunity to engage
with trainers at the end of the process to review their strategies.
Outputs: 20 trainers trained to run sessions on online video strategy. 40 video stories produced
with the support of fellowships.
Activity 4 - Online Video Training Fellowships
Following on directly from Activity 3, TOT participants will be supported to run their own

Investing in Youth
Duration: August 2021-2024
Implementing organization: JHPIEGO
Planned Funding: USD 10-15 million over four years
Background
India has the largest cohort of young people in history. 243 million adolescents (120
million girls) in India continue to face severe disadvantages, despite recent progress in increasing
the age of marriage and reducing gender disparities in education. COVID has further exacerbated
this. An essential part of USAID's portfolio focuses on enabling Young Populations (youth in
age group 10-29 years) to make informed decisions on their health and well-being, and ensuring
information and access to a range of reproductive health services and products is available to
them. Investing in programming for these YPs is critical to build a healthy productive adult
population.
Goal/Purpose
•
Support the Young people of India to realize their full potential by making informed and
responsible decisions for their health and wellbeing. The program looks at working with
early adolescents 10 - 14 years & Young people 15 - 29 years, with a focus on lower socio-
economic categories and a special focus on vulnerable women and girls.
Key strategies
• Advocacy: Bring voices and needs of adolescents and youth on various issues to national
stakeholders, creating a stronger narrative for investing in young people by government
and private sector alike
• Technical Assistance: Improving access to information and services for adolescents and
young people, including for reproductive health services.
• Partnerships: Leverage cross-sectoral partnerships that empowers decision making
among adolescents and young people through improved access to leadership skills,
employability, scholarship programs, skilling and opportunities to engage with young
workforce
• Evidence generation: Build capacity of local organizations for analysis of emerging
evidence and research that can inform advocacy and policies for young people
• Incubation of new solutions: Develop innovative platforms to demonstrate new
ideas/solutions, that reach adolescents and young people to provide information and
services on reproductive health, menstrual hygiene, livelihoods, career development. The
program would explore Grand Challenge/innovation fund as an approach to crowd source
innovative solutions and partnerships.
• Acceleration of existing solutions for scale-up: This would include acceleration of
enterprise-driven solutions for improved access to quality products and services and
improve affordability of products (as an example menstrual hygiene products)
Anticipated Outcomes
• Strengthened health outcomes amongst communities by focusing on empowerment of
young people specially women and girls

• Increased agency of adolescents and young populations to demand for and access
solutions that enable them to make positive choices for themselves. This includes
activities that address adolescent well-being and empowerment more holistically such as
career development, skilling and livelihoods.
• Improved accessibility and affordability of quality FP/RH care/products for adolescents
and young people including menstrual hygiene and contraception
• Strengthened youth friendly ecosystem by increased community/ policy support for
adolescents/young people's well being
Potential collaboration opportunities
1. USAID and Facebook could potentially co-partner on an 'Adolescent/young people
Innovation platform': The needs identified through the youth voices will inspire the ideation
of solutions. We can also co-fund the winning innovative solutions that address the needs of
adolescents/young people. The innovation platform will aim to demonstrate new
ideas/solutions or scale up existing ones. This may include digital solutions, innovations using
virtual reality, Artificial Intelligence, apps, chatbots, IVRS/ helpline, gaming solutions, social
media tools etc. The platform will also demonstrate enterprise-driven solutions for improved
access to quality products and services (such as epharmacy, digital apps, social enterprises for
menstrual hygiene/ contraceptives). Youth voices will inform and guide the platform on
solutions that meet their needs.
2. USAID and Facebook could explore platforms to develop/support the youth champions to
build leadership skills, linking them to career opportunities and livelihoods. While youth led
advocacy will help to understand youth needs and enhance their voices in decision making,
this would also ensure that the youth are given the skills and the opportunity to enhance their
employability and decision making skills.
3. We welcome any other ideas that can help young people have a stronger voice that can help
amplify their needs/demands for youth friendly services and products.

Best practices on our platforms so that you and your team can take advantage of all the tools
available.
• Any of the programs we will deploy as part of our commitment to the Partnership for Central

Thank you.
Activities in Central America
As mentioned, we have an increasing commitment to the development of Central America and a greater
role in the Partnership for Central America. Below, we'd like to share additional information on the
programs we will deploy. These aim to support entrepreneurs and small business owners; and empower
youth to thrive in the digital era.
Programs to support entrepreneurs and small business owners
Over the next three years we will deliver the following programs to provide free digital skills training to
entrepreneurs and small business owners in Central America, enabling them to harness our apps to
connect with their customers:
• MetaBoost: a free comprehensive training program aimed at entrepreneurs and small business
owners in order to build and drive their digital skills to support their economic growth. The
program can be delivered in a hybrid model, online and through in-person training sessions. The
site is available in an array of languages, and you will automatically see it in the language you
have set up.
• #SheMeansBusiness (site in Spanish): our long-term commitment to women's economic
empowerment. This program supports women-owned enterprises to enter the digital economy
through skills training and business inspiration. In 2020, we expanded its scope and added
training on business resiliency through financial education. The training resources for this

program are free and can be accessed in English and Spanish and several other languages all
around the world.
Programs to empower youth to thrive in the digital era
With the following programs, young people will be able to acquire a variety of skills, including digital
literacy, digital marketing, and the use of XR technologies, that will help them harness the opportunity of
the digital revolution:
• We Think Digital (site in Spanish): this program provides resources to build a global community
of responsible digital citizens equipped with the necessary skills to thrive in a digital world. It was
developed in collaboration with experts, academics, non-governmental organizations (NGOs),
and civil society organizations across the globe. Our resources are designed to foster responsible
citizenship and are available in both English and Spanish.
• Meta Blueprint: our learning platform with hundreds of fast, free, self-guided online courses to
help businesses build their marketing skills and take advantage of the tools available to them
across our platforms.
Elections and Integrity Efforts
We are committed to protecting Election Integrity all over the world. Over the last few years, we have
made significant investments in teams and technologies to better protect elections, provide
transparency, empower people to vote, and create safe technologies. To achieve this, we have taken
significant steps to prevent election interference, fight misinformation and increase transparency:
• Our security teams investigate and take down coordinated networks of inauthentic accounts,
Pages and Groups that seek to manipulate public debate. This year, we shared our pilot guarterly
adversarial threat report that provides a broad view into the risks we see worldwide and across
multiple policy violations (see version in Spanish here). Our next quarterly threat report will be
published August 4.
• In October 2021, a month before the elections in Nicaragua, we removed a network of
896 Facebook accounts, 132 Pages, 24 Groups and 362 Instagram accounts in Nicaragua.
This operation targeted domestic audiences in that country and was linked to the
government of Nicaragua and the Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN) party. We
found one portion of this network through our internal investigation into suspected
coordinated inauthentic behavior in the region, and another portion - as a result of
reviewing public reporting about some of this activity. More information in our October
2021 Coordinated Inauthentic Behavior Report.
Also in 2021, we removed 12 Facebook accounts, 172 Pages and 11 accounts on
Instagram of a network that originated primarily in Mexico and targeted audiences in
Honduras, Ecuador, El Salvador, the Dominican Republic and Mexico. We found this
activity as a result of reviewing public reporting about some of this activity. More
information in our December 2021 Coordinated Inauthentic Behavior Report.

• This year, we removed 233 Facebook accounts, 84 Pages, two Groups, and 27 Instagram
accounts for violating our policy against coordinated inauthentic behavior. This network
originated in Costa Rica and El Salvador and targeted primarily Costa Rica and El
Salvador. We found this network after reviewing public reporting about an off-platform
portion of this activity and took action ahead of the election in Costa Rica.
• We work closely with civil society organizations that are critical partners in helping us better
understand the impact of our platforms and the context of the diverse communities in which we
operate around the globe. We've built the Trusted Partner program to foster this partnership
with civil society, strengthen the social media monitoring capacity of local organizations and
improve our policies, enforcement processes, and products to help keep users safe on our
platforms.
• Through our Third-Party Fact-Checking Program we help prevent the spread of misinformation
and provide additional context so people can make informed decisions. We work with
independent, third-party fact-checking organizations who are certified through the non-partisan
International Fact-Checking Network (IFCN) to identify, review and take action on this content. A
map of our fact-checking partners can be found here.
• We provide an industry-leading level of transparency around political advertising and pages. Our
Ads Transparency Tools are available globally for advertisers who want to place ads about social
issues, elections or politics thanks to which these now require authorization and include "Paid
for by" disclaimers. Recently, we announced the expansion of these tools to 19 additional
countries in Latin America.
• We maintain a dedicated team to prevent abuse in WhatsApp focused on three lines of effort:
maintaining the private nature of WhatsApp, preventing coordinated misuse of WhatsApp, and
empowering users to counteract misinformation. The detailed actions we have taken regarding
WhatsApp can be found here.
• We build strategic partnerships around the region to support the integrity of electoral processes.
For example:
• We signed a Cooperation Agreement with the Organization of American States to
continue improving responses to issues such as disinformation, electoral integrity,
freedom of expression and the protection of human rights defenders, in pursuit of
having an increasingly plural online and offline debate.
This year, we partnered with the Electoral Authority of Costa Rica (TSE) and the local
chapter of the United Nations to launched a safety guide to counter political violence
against women. Likewise, in 2021 in Mexico, we partnered with the Electoral Authority
(INE) and the local chapter of the United Nations to launch #SheLeads, a guide that
includes safety tools and best practices for building communities on Facebook, as well as
steps to take to report harassment; and an Instagram Safety Guide for Women in Politics.
Towards the upcoming elections in Brazil, we are working with the Electoral Authority to
protect the democratic process, identify and act on threats and help people gain access
to reliable information about the vote. As part of this work, we will be directing people
using Facebook and Instagram in Brazil to official information about the voting system
and articles countering misinformation about the electoral process.

Finally, our Community Standards aim to find the right balance between giving people a place to express
themselves and promoting a welcoming and safe environment for everyone. In our Transparency Center
we detail the actions taken to create our policies, remove problematic content, reduce its distribution
and inform people. A comprehensive explanation of our Community Standards can be found in this post.
We have alsomade numerous efforts to give people control over what they share, who they share it
with, the content they see and experience, and who can contact them. In our Safety Center you may find
additional information on these actions as well as resources.
Recently, we launched our First Annual Human Rights Report on how we're addressing our human rights
impacts, including insights and actions from our human rights due diligence on products, countries and
responses to emerging crises. As well as our work protecting the privacy of journalists and human rights
defenders, increasing youth safety on Instagram, fighting exploitation across our apps and protecting
free and fair elections around the world.
Again, if you wish to go into greater detail in any of the topics below, we would be happy to set up a call
for the specific issue. Thank you.

authoritarianism, stand for accountable and open government, and advance fairness and
freedom both at home and abroad.

democracies; renew commitments and initiatives to build on that momentum; reaffirm the

lives.

Scaling up COVID-19 emergency prevention and response efforts in India
Duration: June 2021-July 2022
Implementing organization: UNICEF
USG Funding: USD $ 2 million
Background
The current COVID-19 emergency in India is being exacerbated by widespread mis/dis-information and
associated stigma and discrimination causing social divides. USAID is funding UNICEF/India to implement
activities which contribute to the Government of India's comprehensive COVID-19 Risk Communication
and Community Engagement Strategy aimed at further intensifying efforts to strengthen COVID
prevention behaviors, dispel myths, associated stigma and dis/misinformation related to COVID-19
disease.
Goal/Purpose
To provide support to national, state and municipal risk communication and community engagement
campaigns promoting Covid appropriate behaviors (CAB) such as masking, handwashing and social
distancing, and CAB Plus behaviors that address new and emerging needs such as home isolation,
nutrition for COVID effected, danger signs to seek immediate medical care, COVID in children, psycho-
social support to affected families etc. This program is also envisaged to strengthen RCCE preparations
for the impending 3rd and 4th wave of COVID-19.
Key strategies
• 360-degree multi-media campaign: Fatigue around COVID related messaging necessitates that we
reposition our communication approach through a national 360 degree campaign that responds to
urgent pandemic needs and scales-up CAB and CAB Plus behaviors outlined above. This campaign will
cover the development of communication, training packages, mass media such
as radio, print,
social/digital media, offline/online social listening and some mass media programs.
• Enhanced Capacity Building: Orient and train a variety of stakeholders for the implementation of
communications actions in both urban and rural areas such as frontline workers, Self Help Groups,
faith-based organizations, youth networks. Use virtual and in person capacity building opportunities
to train them on counselling skills to reach out to families with key prevention messages. Enrolling
community volunteers as change makers and positive role models for increased adoption of COVID
appropriate behaviors.
• Engaging non-traditional platforms and partners in rural and urban areas: Identify and engage non-
traditional partners, platforms such as edutainment, using artists federations, tribal leaders, state
specific cultural groups and urban local bodies to promote COVID appropriate behaviors such as
masking, handwashing, timely testing, isolating, managing mild cases at home, and accessing
services.
Outcomes
By assisting the Government of India to scale-up and intensify its comprehensive RCCE strategy,
UNICEF's activities described above are expected to contribute to ongoing efforts to reduce the current
accelerated rate of COVID-19 infections, particularly among high-risk communities and strengthen
preparations for future waves.

Opportunities
1. Collaboration with Facebook for an intensive Social media campaign for influencing behaviors
2. Using social media tools for field level capacity building will help enhance reach and impact
3. Actively monitor social media and mainstream media to identify any misinformation and clarify
sources for authentic information
4. Track rumors through social media and interactive media (radio call-in shows, hotlines,
interactive voice and response (IVR) etc). to inform and shape the Government of India
communication strategy on vaccines.

Background
During their recent meeting, Administrator Power and YouTube CEO Susan Wojcicki discussed
the potential of a formal partnership to support independent journalists through leveraging
YouTube's revenue sharing model and platform. Given the success of independent and
mainstream journalists on YouTube across nearly all geographies, and USAID's support for civil
society and independent media around the world, we are seeking to develop and launch a
formal partnership between our organizations in H2 2022, to advance our shared objectives.
Proposal
Given these shared values and interests, YouTube and USAID are launching an independent
media partnership program to support independent media across the world. This program is
dedicated to spotlighting and growing independent media on our platform, by giving them
access to resources and training to help them thrive on YouTube. Elements of this support
could include: grant funding; technical assistance; SPM management; and other training from
YouTube and USAID.
To kick off the program, USAID, in close coordination with their civil society partners around the
world, will nominate a select number of independent journalists in critical regions to participate
in the program. Participants will be invited to a kick-off training summit co-hosted by YouTube
and USAID, for extensive technical and substantive training including "How Youtube Works."
Prominent civil society organizations and independent media experts could also attend and
speak about best practices and business models and principles in launching sustainable media
businesses.
We will announce the program with high-level press engagements (press release, statements,
recorded video messages etc) from USAID Administrator Samantha Power, and YouTube CEO

similar high-level event.
Once the concept is proven, the program will be scaled in 2023 to include additional journalists
